entries.meaning: ‘Whom has not the collapse caused by the qualities afflicted? No one has renounced the intoxicating pride of honour for good. Whom has the fever of youth not overpowered, and whose fame has possessiveness not destroyed? Whom has envy not stained, and whom has the wind of grief not shaken? Whom has the serpent of anxiety not bitten? Who in the world has Maya not pervaded? Bodies are wood and wishes are worms—what steadfast person has not been touched by their woodworm? The three cravings—for children, wealth and reputation—whose understanding have they not soiled? All these form Maya's family, mighty and immeasurable beyond description. Shiva and Brahma fear her; how much account can lesser creatures be?’

‘The very Maya that makes the entire world dance, whose ways no one can discern, dances with her whole troupe, lord of birds, like an actress at the mere play of that Lord's brows. That very Rama is the solid fullness of being, consciousness and bliss, unborn, the embodiment of realization and abode of strength; all-pervading and the pervaded, indivisible and infinite, the Lord of all with unfailing power; beyond qualities, immeasurable and beyond the reach of speech, all-seeing, faultless and unconquered; without possessiveness, form or delusion, eternal, stainless and a mass of joy; beyond Prakriti, dwelling in every heart, Brahman without need, passionless and imperishable. There is no cause for delusion here. Can darkness ever go before the sun?’

‘Such is Raghupati's divine play, enemy of serpents: it bewilders demons and brings his servants joy. Those with impure understanding, enslaved to sense-objects and desire, impute delusion to the Lord in this way. When a person has an eye disorder, he says the moon is yellow. In whatever direction one who is disoriented turns, lord of birds, he says the sun has risen in the west. A person aboard a moving boat sees the world move and, deluded, counts himself still. Children spin around but say that the houses are spinning, calling one another liars. Such delusion concerning Hari, bird, has not the slightest occasion in ignorance, even in a dream. Dull and luckless people under Maya have many curtains drawn across their hearts; stubbornly they voice doubts and place their own ignorance upon Rama.’

‘Hear Raghupati's majesty, lord of birds, as I tell the lovely account according to my understanding: the entire story of how I became deluded about the Lord. You are a recipient of Rama's grace, dear one, and your love of Hari's virtues gives me joy; therefore I hide nothing from you but sing this supremely enchanting secret. Hear Rama's innate nature: he lets no pride remain in his servant. Pride is the root of transmigration, a source of many torments and giver of every grief; therefore the treasure of grace removes it, for his affection for his servant is immense. It is like a wound on an infant's body, Master, which a mother has cut open with a stern heart.’

‘Lord of birds, I shall tell of my own dullness and Rama's grace; listen attentively. Whenever Rama takes a human body and performs many divine deeds for his devotees, I go to Ayodhya, delight in watching his childhood acts, see the birth festival, and remain there for five years, captivated. My chosen deity is Rama as a child, whose bodily beauty equals hundreds of millions of Loves. Enemy of serpents, gazing again and again upon my Lord's face, I make my eyes fruitful. In a small crow's body I stay with Hari and watch his many-coloured childhood play. Wherever he wanders in childhood, there I fly beside him; I pick up and eat whatever morsels fall in the courtyard. Once Raghubira enacted extraordinary deeds beyond all his play; remembering that divine sport, my body thrilled.’

Bhushundi said, ‘Hear, lord of birds, Rama's deeds, which bring his servants joy. The king's palace was beautiful in every way, inlaid with gold and many kinds of gems. Its lovely courtyard cannot be described; all four brothers played there each day. Raghuraya played childish games and roamed the courtyard, bringing his mothers joy. His tender, emerald-dark body held the beauty of many Loves in every limb. His soft, crimson feet were like fresh lotuses, and the lovely nails born of those feet eclipsed the moon's radiance. On his soles were four graceful marks including thunderbolt and banner; lovely anklets made a sweet sound. A charming gold-and-gem ornament had been fashioned for him, and a melodious tinkling girdle graced his waist.’

‘His reddish palms and charming fingernails, long arms with beautiful ornaments; shoulders like a young lion's, conch-like neck, lovely chin and a face that was beauty's very limit. His prattling speech and crimson lips, two pearly, excellent little teeth in each row; graceful cheeks and lovely nose, and a smile as joy-giving as moonbeams. His blue-lotus eyes liberated from worldly existence, while a gorocana mark shone on his forehead. His arched brows and matching ears were lovely; curly black hair spread beauty around him. A thin yellow infant's tunic adorned his body; his delighted babbling and glances enchanted me. The mass of beauty roaming the royal courtyard would dance on seeing his reflection. He played all kinds of games with me—telling them makes me deeply embarrassed. Babbling, he would run to catch me; when I flew off, he would show me a cake.’

‘As I recalled this much, lord of birds, Maya impelled by Raghupati spread over me. That Maya did not cause me the suffering of transmigration as it does other beings. Master, there was another reason here; listen carefully, knower of Hari. Sita's Lord alone possesses undivided knowledge, while every moving and unmoving creature is subject to Maya. If the same uniform knowledge dwelt in all, tell me, what distinction would there be between Lord and creature? The proud creature is subject to Maya; Maya, treasury of the qualities, is subject to the Lord. The creature depends on another, the Lord on himself; creatures are many, Shri's beloved is one. Although the distinction Maya makes is ultimately false, it cannot disappear without Hari, even by millions of means.’

‘Just so, lord of birds, without worshipping Hari a creature's afflictions do not end. Ignorance does not pervade Hari's servant; at the Lord's prompting, knowledge pervades him. Therefore the servant is not destroyed, and awareness of distinction increases his devotion, finest bird. Seeing me astonished by delusion, Rama laughed; now hear the special deed that followed. No one knew the secret of that wonder—not his younger brothers, nor even mother and father. He ran on hands and knees to catch me, his dark body with reddish hands and feet. Then, enemy of serpents, I fled; Rama stretched out his arm to seize me. The farther I flew through the sky, the more I saw Hari's arm remaining close beside me.’

‘Terrified, I shut my eyes; when I looked again I found myself in Kosala's city. Rama saw me and smiled; as he laughed, I instantly went inside his mouth. Within his belly, hear me, king of egg-born creatures, I saw multitudes of universes. There were countless exceedingly wondrous realms, each creation more astonishing than the last; millions of Brahmas and Shivas, innumerable constellations, suns and moons; innumerable guardians of worlds, Yamas and Times, countless mountains and vast earths; boundless oceans, rivers, lakes and forests, creation extended in manifold ways; gods, sages, siddhas, nagas, humans and kinnaras, and all four kinds of moving and unmoving life.’
